claim: The Rec-Seq approach allows simultaneous monitoring of ribosomal 48S preinitiation complex (PIC) formation on every mRNA in the translatome in an in vitro reconstituted system.
source: We have developed a deep sequencing-based approach, Rec-Seq, that allows simultaneous monitoring of ribosomal 48S preinitiation complex (PIC) formation on every mRNA in the translatome in an in vitro reconstituted system.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the development and capability of the Rec-Seq method.

claim: Rec-Seq isolates key early steps in translation initiation in the absence of all other cellular components and processes.
source: Rec-Seq isolates key early steps in translation initiation in the absence of all other cellular components and processes.
evidence: The abstract describes the isolation capability of the Rec-Seq system.

claim: Ded1 promotes 48S PIC formation on the start codons of >1000 native mRNAs.
source: Using this approach, we show that the DEAD-box ATPase Ded1 promotes 48S PIC formation on the start codons of >1000 native mRNAs, most of which have long, structured 5′-untranslated regions (5′UTRs).
evidence: The abstract presents a quantitative finding from the Rec-Seq experiments.

claim: Most mRNAs stimulated by Ded1 have long, structured 5′-untranslated regions (5′UTRs).
source: Using this approach, we show that the DEAD-box ATPase Ded1 promotes 48S PIC formation on the start codons of >1000 native mRNAs, most of which have long, structured 5′-untranslated regions (5′UTRs).
evidence: The abstract characterizes the mRNAs affected by Ded1.

claim: Initiation measured in Rec-Seq was enhanced by Ded1 for most mRNAs previously shown to be highly Ded1-dependent by ribosome profiling of ded1 mutants in vivo.
source: Remarkably, initiation measured in Rec-Seq was enhanced by Ded1 for most mRNAs previously shown to be highly Ded1-dependent by ribosome profiling of ded1 mutants in vivo, demonstrating that the core translation functions of the factor are recapitulated in the purified system.
evidence: The abstract compares in vitro Rec-Seq results with previous in vivo ribosome profiling data.

claim: The core translation functions of Ded1 are recapitulated in the purified system.
source: Remarkably, initiation measured in Rec-Seq was enhanced by Ded1 for most mRNAs previously shown to be highly Ded1-dependent by ribosome profiling of ded1 mutants in vivo, demonstrating that the core translation functions of the factor are recapitulated in the purified system.
evidence: The abstract draws a conclusion about the validity of the in vitro system based on comparison with in vivo data.

claim: Ded1 functions by directly promoting mRNA recruitment to the 43S PIC and scanning to locate the main start codon.
source: Our data do not support a model in which Ded1acts by reducing initiation at alternative start codons in 5′UTRs and instead indicate it functions by directly promoting mRNA recruitment to the 43S PIC and scanning to locate the main start codon.
evidence: The abstract presents a mechanistic conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: The data do not support a model in which Ded1 acts by reducing initiation at alternative start codons in 5′UTRs.
source: Our data do not support a model in which Ded1acts by reducing initiation at alternative start codons in 5′UTRs and instead indicate it functions by directly promoting mRNA recruitment to the 43S PIC and scanning to locate the main start codon.
evidence: The abstract explicitly rejects an alternative mechanistic model.

claim: eIF4A is required for efficient PIC assembly on almost all mRNAs, regardless of their structural complexity.
source: We also provide evidence that eIF4A, another essential DEAD-box initiation factor, is required for efficient PIC assembly on almost all mRNAs, regardless of their structural complexity, in contrast to the preferential stimulation by Ded1 of initiation on mRNAs with long, structured 5′UTRs.
evidence: The abstract presents findings about eIF4A function.

claim: eIF4A's requirement for PIC assembly contrasts with the preferential stimulation by Ded1 of initiation on mRNAs with long, structured 5′UTRs.
source: We also provide evidence that eIF4A, another essential DEAD-box initiation factor, is required for efficient PIC assembly on almost all mRNAs, regardless of their structural complexity, in contrast to the preferential stimulation by Ded1 of initiation on mRNAs with long, structured 5′UTRs.
evidence: The abstract compares the functions of eIF4A and Ded1.

claim: Translation initiation in eukaryotes begins with the assembly of the 43S preinitiation complex (PIC).
source: Translation initiation in eukaryotes begins with the assembly of the 43S preinitiation complex (PIC), containing the small (40S) ribosomal subunit bound to the eIF2∙GTP∙Met-tRNAi ternary complex and several initiation factors (eIFs), including eIF1, eIF1A, eIF5, eIF4B, and eIF3.
evidence: The introduction provides established knowledge about translation initiation.

claim: The 43S PIC contains the small (40S) ribosomal subunit bound to the eIF2∙GTP∙Met-tRNAi ternary complex and several initiation factors (eIFs), including eIF1, eIF1A, eIF5, eIF4B, and eIF3.
source: Translation initiation in eukaryotes begins with the assembly of the 43S preinitiation complex (PIC), containing the small (40S) ribosomal subunit bound to the eIF2∙GTP∙Met-tRNAi ternary complex and several initiation factors (eIFs), including eIF1, eIF1A, eIF5, eIF4B, and eIF3.
evidence: The introduction describes the composition of the 43S PIC based on established knowledge.

claim: The 43S PIC binds the 5′ end of m7G-capped mRNAs with the assistance of the cap-binding protein complex eIF4F.
source: The 43S PIC binds the 5′ end of m7G-capped mRNAs with the assistance of the cap-binding protein complex eIF4F, comprised of cap-binding subunit eIF4E, scaffolding and mRNA-binding subunit eIF4G, and DEAD-box RNA helicase eIF4A.
evidence: The introduction describes the mechanism of mRNA binding based on established knowledge.

claim: eIF4F is comprised of cap-binding subunit eIF4E, scaffolding and mRNA-binding subunit eIF4G, and DEAD-box RNA helicase eIF4A.
source: The 43S PIC binds the 5′ end of m7G-capped mRNAs with the assistance of the cap-binding protein complex eIF4F, comprised of cap-binding subunit eIF4E, scaffolding and mRNA-binding subunit eIF4G, and DEAD-box RNA helicase eIF4A.
evidence: The introduction describes the composition of eIF4F based on established knowledge.

claim: The 43S∙mRNA complex, or 48S PIC, scans the 5′-untranslated region (5′UTR) for a suitable start codon.
source: The resulting 43S∙mRNA complex, or 48S PIC, scans the 5′-untranslated region (5′UTR) for a suitable start codon, whose selection triggers release of most of the initiation factors.
evidence: The introduction describes the scanning process based on established knowledge.

claim: Start codon selection triggers release of most of the initiation factors.
source: The resulting 43S∙mRNA complex, or 48S PIC, scans the 5′-untranslated region (5′UTR) for a suitable start codon, whose selection triggers release of most of the initiation factors.
evidence: The introduction describes the consequence of start codon recognition based on established knowledge.

claim: Joining of the large (60S) ribosomal subunit to the 40S∙Met-tRNAi complex forms the 80S initiation complex.
source: Subsequent joining of the large (60S) ribosomal subunit to the 40S∙Met-tRNAi complex, with the aid of eIF1A and the GTPase factor eIF5B, forms the 80S initiation complex, poised to begin the elongation phase of protein synthesis (Hinnebusch, 2014).
evidence: The introduction describes the subunit joining step with citation to prior work.

claim: The efficiency of translation initiation on specific mRNAs is strongly influenced by the secondary structures in the 5′UTR and the length of the 5′UTR.
source: The efficiency of translation initiation on specific mRNAs is strongly influenced by the secondary structures in the 5′UTR and the length of the 5′UTR (Sonenberg and Hinnebusch, 2009; Niederer et al., 2022).
evidence: The introduction cites prior work establishing the influence of 5′UTR features on translation.

claim: It is believed that the inhibitory structures in mRNA 5′UTRs are resolved by DEAD/H-box RNA helicases.
source: It is believed that the inhibitory structures in mRNA 5′UTRs are resolved by DEAD/H-box RNA helicases (Hinnebusch, 2014).
evidence: The introduction cites a model from prior work about helicase function.

claim: eIF4A is required for the efficient recruitment of a variety of mRNAs tested in vitro regardless of their degrees of structure.
source: However, we and others have demonstrated that eIF4A is required for the efficient recruitment of a variety of mRNAs tested in vitro regardless of their degrees of structure (Pestova and Kolupaeva, 2002; Yourik et al., 2017).
evidence: The introduction cites prior in vitro work on eIF4A function.

claim: Profiling of translating 80S ribosomes in vivo (Ribo-Seq analysis) in an eIF4A temperature-sensitive yeast mutant (tif1-ts) revealed that eIF4A inactivation reduced the relative translation efficiencies of less than 40 mRNAs.
source: Consistent with this, profiling of translating 80S ribosomes in vivo (Ribo-Seq analysis) in an eIF4A temperature-sensitive yeast mutant (tif1-ts) revealed that eIF4A inactivation reduced the relative translation efficiencies of less than 40 mRNAs, despite a strong reduction in bulk polysome assembly (Sen et al., 2015), thus suggesting that the majority of mRNAs have similarly strong requirements for eIF4A in yeast cells.
evidence: The introduction cites prior Ribo-Seq data on eIF4A mutant.

claim: The majority of mRNAs have similarly strong requirements for eIF4A in yeast cells.
source: Consistent with this, profiling of translating 80S ribosomes in vivo (Ribo-Seq analysis) in an eIF4A temperature-sensitive yeast mutant (tif1-ts) revealed that eIF4A inactivation reduced the relative translation efficiencies of less than 40 mRNAs, despite a strong reduction in bulk polysome assembly (Sen et al., 2015), thus suggesting that the majority of mRNAs have similarly strong requirements for eIF4A in yeast cells.
evidence: The introduction draws an inference from cited Ribo-Seq data.

claim: Mammalian eIF4A has been suggested to remodel the 40S subunit to enhance PIC attachment to mRNAs and function beyond its role in RNA unwinding.
source: Mammalian eIF4A has been suggested to remodel the 40S subunit to enhance PIC attachment to mRNAs and function beyond its role in RNA unwinding (Sokabe and Fraser, 2017) and might facilitate the threading of the 5′ end of mRNA into the 40S entry channel (Kumar et al., 2016).
evidence: The introduction cites prior work proposing a mechanism for eIF4A.

claim: eIF4A might facilitate the threading of the 5′ end of mRNA into the 40S entry channel.
source: Mammalian eIF4A has been suggested to remodel the 40S subunit to enhance PIC attachment to mRNAs and function beyond its role in RNA unwinding (Sokabe and Fraser, 2017) and might facilitate the threading of the 5′ end of mRNA into the 40S entry channel (Kumar et al., 2016).
evidence: The introduction cites prior work proposing a speculative mechanism for eIF4A.

claim: Inactivation of yeast DEAD-box helicase Ded1 in a cold-sensitive mutant (ded1-cs) reduced the relative TEs of more than 1100 mRNAs in Ribo-Seq experiments.
source: In contrast to eIF4A, inactivation of yeast DEAD-box helicase Ded1 in a cold-sensitive mutant (ded1-cs) was found to reduce the relative TEs of more than 1100 mRNAs in Ribo-Seq experiments (Sen et al., 2015; Sen et al., 2019).
evidence: The introduction cites prior Ribo-Seq data on Ded1 mutant.

claim: Ded1-hyperdependent mRNAs displayed a marked tendency for long and structured 5′UTRs.
source: These Ded1-hyperdependent mRNAs displayed a marked tendency for long and structured 5′UTRs (Sen et al., 2015).
evidence: The introduction cites prior characterization of Ded1-hyperdependent mRNAs.

claim: Profiling of small (40S) ribosomal subunits in the ded1-cs mutant provided evidence that Ded1 stimulates the translation of Ded1-hyperdependent mRNAs by promoting attachment of 43S PICs to the mRNA 5′ ends or subsequent scanning to the start codon.
source: Profiling of small (40S) ribosomal subunits in the ded1-cs mutant provided evidence that Ded1 stimulates the translation of Ded1-hyperdependent mRNAs by promoting attachment of 43S PICs to the mRNA 5′ ends or subsequent scanning to the start codon (Sen et al., 2019).
evidence: The introduction cites prior 40S profiling data supporting a mechanistic model.

claim: In a purified yeast translation initiation system several mRNAs identified as being hyperdependent on Ded1 in vivo also displayed greater stimulation by Ded1 of 48S PIC assembly than observed for either Ded1-hypodependent mRNAs or variants of the hyperdependent mRNAs lacking their 5′UTR secondary structures.
source: Furthermore, in a purified yeast translation initiation system several mRNAs identified as being hyperdependent on Ded1 in vivo also displayed greater stimulation by Ded1 of 48S PIC assembly than observed for either Ded1-hypodependent mRNAs or variants of the hyperdependent mRNAs lacking their 5′UTR secondary structures (Gupta et al., 2018).
evidence: The introduction cites prior in vitro work validating in vivo findings.

claim: Ded1 is important particularly for stimulating translation of mRNAs that have long, structured 5′UTRs.
source: Together, these findings suggest that Ded1 is important particularly for stimulating translation of mRNAs that have long, structured 5′UTRs.
evidence: The introduction draws a conclusion from multiple cited studies.

claim: Ded1 activity on mRNAs with long, structured 5′UTRs is enhanced by interaction of its N-terminal domain with eIF4A and eIF4E, and of its C-terminal domain with eIF4G.
source: Several lines of evidence indicate that Ded1 activity on such mRNAs is enhanced by interaction of its N-terminal domain with eIF4A and eIF4E, and of its C-terminal domain with eIF4G (Gao et al., 2016; Gupta et al., 2018; Gulay et al., 2020), indicating functional coupling between eIF4F and Ded1 in 48S PIC assembly.
evidence: The introduction cites prior work on Ded1 protein interactions.

claim: There is functional coupling between eIF4F and Ded1 in 48S PIC assembly.
source: Several lines of evidence indicate that Ded1 activity on such mRNAs is enhanced by interaction of its N-terminal domain with eIF4A and eIF4E, and of its C-terminal domain with eIF4G (Gao et al., 2016; Gupta et al., 2018; Gulay et al., 2020), indicating functional coupling between eIF4F and Ded1 in 48S PIC assembly.
evidence: The introduction draws an inference from cited protein interaction data.

claim: Ded1 broadly promotes scanning through 5′UTRs by blocking initiation at alternative start codons positioned just upstream of secondary structures that are unwound by Ded1 in vivo.
source: Other evidence suggests that Ded1 broadly promotes scanning through 5′UTRs by blocking initiation at alternative start codons positioned just upstream of secondary structures that are unwound by Ded1 in vivo, thus allowing the scanning PIC to continue downstream to the main start codon of the mRNA (Guenther et al., 2018).
evidence: The introduction cites an alternative mechanistic model from prior work.

claim: Ded1 and its mammalian ortholog DDX3 have been implicated in facilitating the joining of the large ribosomal subunit to the 48S PIC after start codon recognition.
source: It appears that Ded1 can regulate translation of mRNAs in vivo in ways ostensibly distinct from its functions in promoting PIC attachment or scanning on structured mRNAs. Ded1 and its mammalian ortholog DDX3 have been implicated in facilitating the joining of the large ribosomal subunit to the 48S PIC after start codon recognition (Geissler et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2022).
evidence: The introduction cites prior work on an additional function of Ded1.

claim: Ded1 can repress translation by segregating mRNAs into phase-separated RNA–protein granules, processing bodies (PBs), or stress granules (SGs), during cell stresses.
source: There is also evidence that Ded1 can repress translation by segregating mRNAs into phase-separated RNA–protein granules, processing bodies (PBs), or stress granules (SGs), during cell stresses.
evidence: The introduction cites prior work on Ded1's role in stress granule formation.

claim: Granule formation in glucose-starved cells is reduced by depletion of Ded1 and is enhanced by Ded1 overexpression or impairment of its ATPase activity in non-starved cells.
source: Granule formation in glucose-starved cells is reduced by depletion of Ded1 and is enhanced by Ded1 overexpression or impairment of its ATPase activity in non-starved cells in a manner regulated by regions in the Ded1 NTD and CTD (Beckham et al., 2008; Hilliker et al., 2011; Hondele et al., 2019).
evidence: The introduction cites prior work on Ded1's role in granule formation.

claim: Ded1 initially forms an inactive complex with eIF4F and mRNA that is stalled at a step upstream of 43S PIC joining and subsequently utilizes ATP hydrolysis to allow progression into the initiation pathway.
source: It was suggested that Ded1 initially forms an inactive complex with eIF4F and mRNA that is stalled at a step upstream of 43S PIC joining and subsequently utilizes ATP hydrolysis to allow progression into the initiation pathway (Beckham et al., 2008; Hilliker et al., 2011).
evidence: The introduction cites a mechanistic model from prior work.

claim: Heat-shock evokes Ded1 sequestration in SGs in a manner antagonized at low temperatures by a polar intrinsically disordered region (IDR) in the Ded1 NTD.
source: Heat-shock also evokes Ded1 sequestration in SGs in a manner antagonized at low temperatures by a polar intrinsically disordered region (IDR) in the Ded1 NTD.
evidence: The introduction describes prior findings on Ded1 behavior during heat shock.

claim: Purified Ded1 displayed heat-induced phase separation in vitro that was enhanced by mRNA and the Ded1 CTD but suppressed by the N-terminal IDR.
source: Purified Ded1 displayed heat-induced phase separation in vitro that was enhanced by mRNA and the Ded1 CTD but suppressed by the N-terminal IDR.
evidence: The introduction describes prior in vitro findings on Ded1 phase separation.

claim: Heat-shock preferentially reduced the TEs of mRNAs with structured 5′UTRs and increased their condensation.
source: Interestingly, heat-shock preferentially reduced the TEs of mRNAs with structured 5′UTRs and increased their condensation, in a manner modulated by the N-terminal IDR, leading to the model that condensation of Ded1 and associated mRNAs preferentially reduces the translation of Ded1-hyperdependent mRNAs with structured 5′UTRs during heat-shock (Iserman et al., 2020).
evidence: The introduction cites prior work on heat shock effects on translation.

claim: Glucose starvation or heat-shock leads to widespread dissociation of Ded1, eIF4A, and eIF4B from the 5′UTRs of mRNAs.
source: Other findings indicate that glucose starvation or heat-shock leads to widespread dissociation of Ded1, eIF4A, and eIF4B from the 5′UTRs of mRNAs (Castelli et al., 2011; Bresson et al., 2020), which could underlie reduced translation of Ded1-hyperdependent mRNAs that remain soluble in stressed cells.
evidence: The introduction cites prior work on factor dissociation during stress.

claim: Ded1-hyperdependent mRNAs vary greatly in their translational suppression during stress.
source: Examining the TE changes conferred by glucose starvation or heat-shock by ribosome profiling suggested that Ded1-hyperdependent mRNAs vary greatly in their translational suppression during stress, which might involve a combinatorial effect of impairing eIF4A, eIF4B, and Ded1 function on the most affected subsets (Sen et al., 2021).
evidence: The introduction cites prior ribosome profiling data on stress responses.

claim: It is possible that Ded1 has additional functions in the nucleus as it appears to shuttle between nucleus and cytoplasm.
source: It is possible that Ded1 has additional functions in the nucleus as it appears to shuttle between nucleus and cytoplasm and interacts both physically and functionally with the nuclear cap-binding proteins (Senissar et al., 2014).
evidence: The introduction speculates about additional Ded1 functions based on cited observations.

claim: Ded1 was found to co-purify with pre-90S and pre-40S immature ribosomes.
source: Ded1 was also found to co-purify with pre-90S and pre-40S immature ribosomes (Schäfer et al., 2003), and thus might function in ribosome biogenesis.
evidence: The introduction cites prior biochemical data on Ded1 interactions.

claim: Ded1 might function in ribosome biogenesis.
source: Ded1 was also found to co-purify with pre-90S and pre-40S immature ribosomes (Schäfer et al., 2003), and thus might function in ribosome biogenesis.
evidence: The introduction speculates about Ded1 function based on cited co-purification data.

claim: The inactivated ded1 mutant protein could have had dominant effects rather than simply producing a loss of Ded1 function.
source: A difficulty with interpreting the previous ribosome profiling experiments with ded1 mutations is that the inactivated mutant protein could have had dominant effects rather than simply producing a loss of Ded1 function.
evidence: The introduction raises a concern about interpretation of prior mutant studies.

claim: It is possible that the ded1 mutations in the catalytic domain analyzed by ribosome profiling led to impaired translation of many Ded1-hyperdependent mRNAs in non-stressed cells owing to their sequestration with the mutant ded1 proteins in condensates inaccessible to the initiation machinery.
source: For example, in view of evidence that inhibition of Ded1 ATPase activity can lead to the formation of translationally inert mRNP granules, it is possible that the ded1 mutations in the catalytic domain analyzed by ribosome profiling led to impaired translation of many Ded1-hyperdependent mRNAs in non-stressed cells owing to their sequestration with the mutant ded1 proteins in condensates inaccessible to the initiation machinery.
evidence: The introduction speculates about potential artifacts in prior mutant studies.

claim: Several mRNAs that were found to be Ded1-hyperdependent in vivo displayed a greater stimulation of 48S PIC assembly by Ded1 compared to several in vivo hypodependent mRNAs in a fully purified system.
source: As noted above, we demonstrated that several mRNAs that were found to be Ded1-hyperdependent in vivo displayed a greater stimulation of 48S PIC assembly by Ded1 compared to several in vivo hypodependent mRNAs in a fully purified system, confirming a direct role of Ded1 in stimulating initiation on these few mRNAs in the soluble phase in the absence of any other cellular proteins besides ribosomes and canonical initiation factors.
evidence: The introduction cites prior in vitro work by the authors.

claim: Many other mRNAs found to be hyperdependent on Ded1 in vivo might not be stimulated directly by Ded1's ability to resolve secondary structures in 5′UTRs and promote PIC recruitment or scanning to the start codon.
source: However, it was possible that many other mRNAs found to be hyperdependent on Ded1 in vivo are not stimulated directly by Ded1's ability to resolve secondary structures in 5′UTRs and promote PIC recruitment or scanning to the start codon.
evidence: The introduction raises a question that motivates the current study.

claim: Stable 48S PIC formation on mRNA start codons was strongly dependent on the 5′-cap in the reconstituted yeast initiation system.
source: In previous work using the reconstituted yeast initiation system, we found that stable 48S PIC formation on mRNA start codons was strongly dependent on the 5′-cap (Mitchell et al., 2010; Yourik et al., 2017).
evidence: The introduction cites prior work by the authors on the reconstituted system.

claim: The cap prevented off-pathway events and enforced a requirement for the full set of initiation factors to efficiently assemble a 48S PIC.
source: The cap also prevented off-pathway events and enforced a requirement for the full set of initiation factors to efficiently assemble a 48S PIC.
evidence: The introduction describes prior findings on the role of the cap in the reconstituted system.

claim: In the reconstituted system 43S PICs are loaded onto the 5′ ends of mRNAs in a cap-dependent manner and they scan from 5′ to 3′ to locate the start codon.
source: These results indicate that in the reconstituted system 43S PICs are loaded onto the 5′ ends of mRNAs in a cap-dependent manner and that they scan from 5′ to 3′ to locate the start codon.
evidence: The introduction draws a conclusion from prior work on the reconstituted system.

claim: Rec-Seq allowed isolation of the crucial and highly regulated series of events leading up to 48S PIC assembly from all later steps of initiation and elongation.
source: Rec-Seq allowed us to isolate the crucial and highly regulated series of events leading up to 48S PIC assembly from all later steps of initiation and elongation.
evidence: The introduction describes a key advantage of the Rec-Seq method.

claim: Processes such as mRNA localization and decay and RNA and protein compartmentalization do not contribute to the outcome of Rec-Seq experiments.
source: Processes such as mRNA localization and decay and RNA and protein compartmentalization, which can complicate in vivo analyses, likewise do not contribute to the outcome of Rec-Seq experiments.
evidence: The introduction describes another advantage of the Rec-Seq method.

claim: Ded1 stimulates 48S PIC assembly on ~1000 mRNAs in the Rec-Seq system.
source: Our studies indicate that in the Rec-Seq system Ded1 stimulates 48S PIC assembly on ~1000 mRNAs.
evidence: The introduction summarizes a key finding from the current study.

claim: Ded1-dependent mRNAs include ~90% of the mRNAs previously found to be hyperdependent on Ded1 in vivo by ribosome profiling of the ded1-cs mutant.
source: These Ded1-dependent mRNAs include ~90% of the mRNAs previously found to be hyperdependent on Ded1 in vivo by ribosome profiling of the ded1-cs mutant.
evidence: The introduction summarizes a key finding comparing in vitro and in vivo results.

claim: The fact that addition of Ded1 stimulates 48S PIC assembly on these mRNAs in the reconstituted Rec-Seq system argues against the involvement of other cellular processes or proteins beyond the core initiation machinery in Ded1 function.
source: The fact that addition of Ded1 stimulates 48S PIC assembly on these mRNAs in the reconstituted Rec-Seq system argues against the involvement of other cellular processes or proteins beyond the core initiation machinery in Ded1 function, and the possibility that the in vivo ribosome profiling results were influenced by dominant negative effects of the ded1-cs mutation or by altered expression or activity of the translational machinery in the mutant cells.
evidence: The introduction draws a conclusion from the comparison of in vitro and in vivo results.

claim: The mRNAs that are strongly dependent on Ded1 in the Rec-Seq system exhibit a high propensity for long and structured 5′UTRs.
source: The mRNAs that are strongly dependent on Ded1 in the Rec-Seq system exhibit a high propensity for long and structured 5′UTRs, providing compelling evidence that Ded1 acts directly to stimulate 48S PIC formation by unwinding 5′UTR structures to facilitate mRNA binding to the PIC and scanning to find the start codon.
evidence: The introduction summarizes a key finding about mRNA features.

claim: Ded1 acts directly to stimulate 48S PIC formation by unwinding 5′UTR structures to facilitate mRNA binding to the PIC and scanning to find the start codon.
source: The mRNAs that are strongly dependent on Ded1 in the Rec-Seq system exhibit a high propensity for long and structured 5′UTRs, providing compelling evidence that Ded1 acts directly to stimulate 48S PIC formation by unwinding 5′UTR structures to facilitate mRNA binding to the PIC and scanning to find the start codon.
evidence: The introduction draws a mechanistic conclusion from the data.

claim: Alternative initiation at upstream start codons is too infrequent, and the suppression of these events by addition of Ded1 too small, to account for the stimulatory effects of Ded1 on 48S PIC assembly in the reconstituted system.
source: Our results also indicate that alternative initiation at upstream start codons is too infrequent, and the suppression of these events by addition of Ded1 too small, to account for the stimulatory effects of Ded1 on 48S PIC assembly in the reconstituted system.
evidence: The introduction summarizes a finding that argues against an alternative model.

claim: eIF4A strongly stimulates the formation of 48S PICs on the vast majority of yeast mRNAs, regardless of their 5′UTR length or degree of secondary structure.
source: Finally, we show that eIF4A strongly stimulates the formation of 48S PICs on the vast majority of yeast mRNAs, regardless of their 5′UTR length or degree of secondary structure, in contrast to the specificity we observe for Ded1 in stimulating recruitment of mRNAs with long, structured 5′UTRs.
evidence: The introduction summarizes findings about eIF4A function.

claim: eIF4A plays a general role in facilitating binding of all mRNAs to the 43S PIC, whereas Ded1 unwinds inhibitory secondary structures to promote PIC binding and scanning on mRNAs with structured 5′UTRs.
source: These data are consistent with the model that eIF4A plays a general role in facilitating binding of all mRNAs to the 43S PIC, whereas Ded1 unwinds inhibitory secondary structures to promote PIC binding and scanning on mRNAs with structured 5′UTRs.
evidence: The introduction presents a mechanistic model based on the data.

claim: A metagene plot of the number of RPF reads versus position of RPF 5′ ends relative to the mAUG codon for each mRNA revealed that the overwhelming majority contain a single peak of RPFs with the bulk of 5′ ends located 12 nt upstream of the mAUG codon.
source: A metagene plot of the number of RPF reads versus position of RPF 5′ ends relative to the mAUG codon for each mRNA revealed that the overwhelming majority contain a single peak of RPFs with the bulk of 5′ ends located 12 nt upstream of the mAUG codon (Figure 1B–D).
evidence: The results section describes data shown in Figure 1B-D.

claim: The position of RPF 5′ ends 12 nt upstream of the mAUG is expected for PICs with the 40S P site containing the AUG start codon base paired with the anticodon of Met-tRNAi.
source: This is the position expected for PICs with the 40S P site containing the AUG start codon base paired with the anticodon of Met-tRNAi (Ingolia et al., 2009; Archer et al., 2016).
evidence: The results section cites prior work to interpret the observed RPF positions.

claim: Groups of ~1000 transcripts among the 3052 for which Rec-Seq data were obtained showed more than twofold increased mRPFs in the presence of 100 or 500 nM Ded1 compared to no added Ded1.
source: We conducted differential expression analysis using the software DESeq2 (Love et al., 2014) to identify mRNAs that exhibit statistically significant changes in normalized RPFs mapping to the main start codon (mRPFs) on addition of Ded1. Groups of ~1000 transcripts among the 3052 for which Rec-Seq data were obtained showed more than twofold increased mRPFs in the presence of 100 or 500 nM Ded1 compared to no added Ded1, whereas only ~100 transcripts showed higher mRPFs at 500 nM versus 100 nM Ded1 (Figure 2A–C, red dots).
evidence: The results section describes DESeq2 analysis results shown in Figure 2A-C.

claim: Only ~100 transcripts showed higher mRPFs at 500 nM versus 100 nM Ded1.
source: Groups of ~1000 transcripts among the 3052 for which Rec-Seq data were obtained showed more than twofold increased mRPFs in the presence of 100 or 500 nM Ded1 compared to no added Ded1, whereas only ~100 transcripts showed higher mRPFs at 500 nM versus 100 nM Ded1 (Figure 2A–C, red dots).
evidence: The results section describes DESeq2 analysis results shown in Figure 2A-C.

claim: Substantially smaller numbers of mRNAs displayed decreased mRPFs as Ded1 concentration was increased (71, 182, and 51 mRNAs, respectively).
source: Substantially smaller numbers of mRNAs displayed decreased mRPFs as Ded1 concentration was increased (Figure 2A–C, dark blue dots; 71, 182, and 51 mRNAs, respectively).
evidence: The results section describes DESeq2 analysis results shown in Figure 2A-C.

claim: 87% of mRNAs showing significant increases in mRPFs at 100 nM Ded1 were also increased at 500 nM Ded1.
source: Importantly, 87% of mRNAs showing significant increases in mRPFs at 100 nM Ded1 were also increased at 500 nM Ded1 (Figure 2D), and 68% of the mRNAs with significantly diminished mRPFs at 100 nM Ded1 were also decreased at 500 nM Ded1 (Figure 2E)—both highly significant overlaps.
evidence: The results section describes overlap analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: 68% of the mRNAs with significantly diminished mRPFs at 100 nM Ded1 were also decreased at 500 nM Ded1.
source: Importantly, 87% of mRNAs showing significant increases in mRPFs at 100 nM Ded1 were also increased at 500 nM Ded1 (Figure 2D), and 68% of the mRNAs with significantly diminished mRPFs at 100 nM Ded1 were also decreased at 500 nM Ded1 (Figure 2E)—both highly significant overlaps.
evidence: The results section describes overlap analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The 1006 mRNAs with significantly increased mRPFs at 500 nM Ded1 had median increases of 3.6-fold and 4.8-fold at 100 and 500 nM Ded1, respectively.
source: The 1006 mRNAs with significantly increased mRPFs at 500 nM Ded1 had median increases of 3.6-fold and 4.8-fold at 100 and 500 nM Ded1, respectively (Figure 2F, cols. 3–4).
evidence: The results section describes quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The 911 mRNAs that had significantly increased mRPFs in 100 nM Ded1 had median increases of 4.1-fold and 5.2-fold at 100 and 500 nM Ded1, respectively.
source: Similarly, the 911 mRNAs that had significantly increased mRPFs in 100 nM Ded1 had median increases of 4.1-fold and 5.2-fold at 100 and 500 nM Ded1, respectively, and the 793 mRNAs common to both sets had median increases of 4.7-fold and 6.1-fold (Figure 2F, cols. 5–8).
evidence: The results section describes quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Ded1 might resolve secondary structures positioned just downstream of the mAUG codon that increase the dwell time of the PIC and increase the probability of PIC assembly versus continued scanning downstream that leads to initiation on iAUG codons.
source: This in turn implies that Ded1 does not inspect the context sequence but rather promotes scanning to reduce the dwell time of the PIC at the AUG similarly for both weak and strong contexts. Rather than invoking leaky scanning, it could be proposed that the RPFs formed at iAUGs originate from a small fraction of mRNA isoforms with transcription initiation sites within the CDSs (Arribere and Gilbert, 2013; Lu and Lin, 2019) that contain the internal initiation sites as the first AUGs encountered on scanning from the cap. Alternatively, the iRPFs could be formed on uncapped mRNAs cleaved at the 5′ end in cells or in vitro, which would require cap-independent initiation. In either case, Ded1 could stimulate PIC assembly at the iAUGs by the same mechanism identified above for canonical mAUGs. Several lines of evidence argue against this possibility and instead favor the Ded1-induced leaky scanning model proposed above. First, the level of iAUG initiation relative to mAUG initiation (RRO) depends strongly on the sequence context surrounding the mAUG (Figure 5O), as expected for the leaky scanning model but inconsistent with a model in which iAUG occupancy arises from 5′-truncated mRNA isoforms or fragments. In addition, mRNAs that have a high level of iAUG occupancy relative to mAUG occupancy (RRO ≥ 0.5) tend to have less secondary structure in the 5′ ends of their coding sequences than do mRNAs with less iAUG occupancy (Figure 5P, cols. 3–8, compare blue and orange boxes), consistent with a model in which secondary structures just downstream of the mAUG inhibit further scanning and diminish mAUG readthrough (Kozak, 1990).
evidence: The results section proposes a mechanistic model and cites prior work.
